summary: Marcus, the narrator, wakes his friend Jolu over secure Xnet chat after learning that radio vans may be watching them. They decide to build a web of trust through a key-signing among trusted friends, disguised as a teenage party so they have an excuse if anyone asks. Jolu proposes the Sutro Baths as the venue. The note closes with a reflection on dealing with a spy by feeding them misinformation rather than exposing them.
one_line: Marcus and Jolu plan a disguised key-signing party at the Sutro Baths to build a trusted encrypted network while evading surveillance.
key_facts: The narrator's closest friends are his ARG team, and he has about 20 or 30 people he can fully vouch for.
The narrator woke Jolu by ringing his cell phone and hanging up after the first ring, three times in a row.
Jolu was sent to a blog post about radio vans and came back worried, asking 'You sure they're looking for us?'
The narrator sent Jolu to a quiz to show the situation was not as bad as he feared.
Web of trust is a cryptographic method in which people exchange keys so they can talk securely with trusted people while others cannot listen in.
Web of trust requires participants to physically meet at least once to get started.
Jolu's idea was to hold a party so that the group would have a ready-made excuse if anyone asked what they were doing there.
Jolu suggested the Sutro Baths as the location for the gathering.
Darryl is someone the group thinks would know how to organize this kind of thing, and he was great at it.
The narrator poses the question of how to hold the key-signing without getting busted.
The passage argues that if you find a spy, exposing or killing them may lead to a more careful replacement spy.
A better approach to a spy, according to the passage, is to intercept their communications and feed them and their masters misinformation.
